evidence: Hang Thiec Street is an ancient street located within Hang Gai ward, Hoan Kiem district, in the city of Hanoi. It is one of the few remaining historic streets in Hanoi that still preserves both the sounds and the traditional craft of metalworking.

It is one of the few remaining historic streets in Hanoi that still preserves both the sounds and the traditional craft of metalworking. In the past, the name of the street originated from its role as a center for handmade tin and lead casting, serving the daily needs and spiritual requirements of the residents of the imperial capital.

Historically, the origins and settlers of Hang Thiec Street can be traced back to the village of Dan Hoi (formerly part of Ha Dong). According to the genealogies of long-standing families like the Tran clan, the founder of the tin-crafting profession was granted the title of "Tich cuc truong," or head of the Tin Management Bureau, by the royal court during the Le dynasty.

Over time, artisans from nearby villages known for their metalwork, such as Phu Thu (now part of Hoai Duc), Thuan Tien, and Bac Ninh, migrated to Hang Thiec Street to establish their businesses, making it a bustling center for manufacturing household goods. During the colonial period, the French authorities respected the local production identity and named the street Rue des Ferblantiers, meaning "Street of Tin Workers." In 1945, the then Governor of Hanoi, Tran Van Lai, officially restored the original Vietnamese name, Hang Thiec Street, which has been maintained until today.
